entities.summary:
Fabius Valens, a Roman military commander from Anagnia, emerged as a pivotal, albeit ultimately tragic, figure during the tumultuous Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE), a period of intense civil strife following Nero's suicide. His strategic acumen and unwavering loyalty to Vitellius were instrumental in the initial ascendancy of the Vitellian faction, plunging the Roman Empire into a brutal succession crisis that reshaped its political landscape and tested the very fabric of imperial authority. Valens's career, marked by ambition and military prowess, underscored the fragility of the nascent Roman principate and the potent influence of individual commanders in an era of political vacuum.

Initially a legate of Legio I Germanica in Germania Inferior, Valens seized the opportunity presented by the widespread discontent with Emperor Galba. In January 69 CE, he led his legions in declaring for Vitellius, the governor of Germania Inferior, as emperor. Valens then marched a formidable army of 40,000 men, comprising legionaries and auxiliaries, across Gaul and the Alps into Italy. His decisive victory alongside Aulus Caecina Alienus at the First Battle of Bedriacum in April 69 CE utterly crushed Otho's forces, paving the way for Vitellius's brief reign. Despite this triumph, Valens's conduct was often marred by accusations of avarice and rapaciousness, alienating potential allies and contributing to the moral decay within Vitellius's camp.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fabius Valens's military leadership and political maneuvering were central to the initial successes of Vitellius, prolonging the civil war and contributing to the instability that ultimately paved the way for the Flavian dynasty. His actions directly impacted the fate of two emperors and the course of Roman imperial succession.
